Publisher XML converted to located text (jats_text): title, figure captions and table captions only; no body paragraphs
pages_convention: XML caption locators (jats_text) exactly as printed (e.g. 'Fig. 6', 'Fig.10', 'Table 5') wherever the XML supplies text. entry.evidence: the geological processes by which the high-grade ores in the ZID were formed remains poorly constrained

sequences.source_document: Published paper PDF (body text) and publisher XML (captions)

steps.action: The authors pose the question of how the high-grade (TFe > 50 wt%) magnetite ores of the Zankan iron deposit formed.
steps.quote: the geological processes by which the high-grade ores in the ZID were formed remains poorly constrained

steps.action: The authors take three published genetic models from the literature as rivals for IF-hosted high-grade ore: syngenetic, supergene/metamorphic, and hypogene-supergene.
steps.quote: It is generally believed that the genesis of high-grade iron ores hosted in IF can be ascribed to one of three models

steps.action: The authors use earlier field observations (Li, 2018, inferred to be the first author's dissertation) of orebody attitude, alteration and contacts to argue that the high-grade ore comes from secondary fluid alteration of the IF.
steps.quote: based on earlier geological observations (Li, 2018), such as orebody attitude, wall rock alteration, and contact relations

steps.action: The authors design a combined geological and geochemical study (petrography, whole-rock chemistry, O and S isotopes, zircon U-Pb and Hf) to separate the ore-forming phases.
steps.quote: Therefore, it is essential to separate the ore forming phases through a combined geological and geochemical study.

steps.action: From field and thin-section petrography and from major and trace elements of 7 high-grade ore and 12 dacite-porphyry samples, the authors define sedimentary T1 and altered T2 ore types and describe IF xenocrysts and magnetite-ferro actinolite veins in the dacite, wall-rock alteration, and T2 REE patterns with negative Eu anomalies like the dacite's (Fig. 3, Fig. 4, Fig. 6, Fig. 7, Fig. 8; Table 1, Table 2).
steps.quote: Based on mineral assemblages, iron ores in the ZID can be classified as two types.

steps.action: Methods: the authors check the reproducibility of the trace-element ICP-MS data against the reference standards FER-1 and FER-2.
steps.quote: Based on the analysis of standards FER-1 and FER-2 external reproducibility is estimated to be 5 to 10%.

steps.action: The authors date zircons from the dacite-porphyry by LA-ICP-MS U-Pb and resolve two concordia groups, 497.82 ± 3.81 Ma (intrusion) and 551.25 ± 3.32 Ma (captured detrital zircons) (Fig.10, p. 13).
steps.quote: One group yields an age of 497.82 ± 3.81 Ma (MSWD = 0.63, n = 6)

steps.action: Methods: the authors run zircon standard 91500 and analyse GJ-1 as an unknown to monitor external uncertainty in the U-Pb analyses.
steps.quote: zircon GJ-1 was analyzed as an unknown throughout the entire analytical procedure to monitor external uncertainties

steps.action: The authors measure δ18O of magnetite from T1 and T2 ores and δ34S of pyrite from T2 ore (Table 5, Table 6).
steps.quote: The oxygen isotope composition (δ18OVSMOW) of the magnetite from T1 and T2 ores range from 1.8 to 3.2‰, and 4.4 to 5.5‰, respectively

steps.action: The authors check their pyrite δ34S values against an independent recent data set from the same deposit and find them consistent.
steps.quote: consistent with a recent study on the ZID (17.2 to 29.89‰, Ding et al., 2021b)

steps.action: The authors compare cross-cutting relations and ages: the vein-free 505 ± 18 Ma granite against the vein-bearing 497.82 Ma dacite. They conclude that T2 ore formed after 497.82 Ma.
steps.quote: the younger zircon group age (497.82 ± 3.81 Ma) is interpreted here to reflect the formation age of the T2 ores

steps.action: Before using immobile-element classification, the authors check from low LOI (0.06-0.19 wt%) and consistent element patterns that the dacite's REE and HFSE are unaltered.
steps.quote: trace elements, such as REE and HFSEs (e.g., Nb, Ta, Zr, Hf, Ti, Th) in the dacite-porphyry, can be considered immobile

steps.action: Using mineralogy, ΣFeO/MgO and Ga/Al discrimination diagrams, the authors exclude S-type and A-type affinities for the dacite-porphyry and classify it as I-type (Fig. 9, p. 12).
steps.quote: the Cambrian dacite-porphyry can be classified as an I-type igneous rock

steps.action: From zircon εHf(t) values and two-stage Hf model ages, the authors infer that the dacite magma came from partial melting of Paleo- to Mesoproterozoic crust (Fig. 11, p. 15).
steps.quote: generated through the partial melting of Paleoproterozoic to Mesoproterozoic crustal material

steps.action: The authors run the Hf standards Mud Tank and GJ-1 with the unknowns and report that the measured 176Hf/177Hf agrees with recommended values.
steps.quote: in good accordance with the recommended values for MC-ICP-MS analysis

steps.action: The authors weigh published rival settings (an extensional rift at ~521 Ma versus a subduction accretionary wedge) and infer a continental-arc setting for the 497.82 Ma I-type dacite (Fig. 12).
steps.quote: was mainly developed in a continental arc volcanic setting where the Proto-Tethys ocean plate was subducted under the TTT

steps.action: The authors compare T1 and T2 REE patterns and δ18O with each other and with published altered-IF ores (Hamersley, Anshan). They conclude that T2 formed by post-depositional fluid alteration, not at the sedimentary stage.
steps.quote: suggesting that significantly different geochemical processes led to the mineralization of T1 and T2 ores

steps.action: Because T2 ore and dacite share REE patterns, the authors pose two rival fluid sources: (a) the dacite magma, or (b) a non-magmatic fluid that leached the dacite.
steps.quote: the mineralizing fluid may be associated with; (a) the dacite-porphyry magma, or (b) a non-magmatic fluid

steps.action: The authors exclude a direct magmatic fluid because pyrite δ34S (19.1-28.2‰) is far heavier than mantle values and close to Cambrian seawater sulfate.
steps.quote: Therefore, it is unlikely that the high-grade iron ore forming fluid was directly derived from the magma.

steps.action: The authors use magnetite oxygen isotopes as a second, independent line, which points to 18O-poor meteoric water rather than a magmatic fluid.
steps.quote: [...] further indicate that the high-grade ore mineralization fluid was not magmatically sourced

steps.action: The authors compare the expected outcome of sulfate reduction of basin-derived sulfate (pyrite δ34S between coeval seawater and gypsum) with their pyrite data and cited gypsum δ34S (Chen, 2012). They also note magmatic H2S input as a possible addition.
steps.quote: leading to the δ34Spyrite that are lower than coeval seawater but higher than δ34Sgypsum values

steps.action: From replacement textures and cited reaction equations R1-R3, the authors infer a reducing, acidic, iron-transporting fluid that leached silica and later precipitated pyrite (Fig. 13, p. 16).
steps.quote: indicates that the initial high-grade ore forming fluid was characterized by reducing, acidic conditions

steps.action: The authors keep a four-stage genetic model of fracture-guided, meteoric-derived fluids leaching silica and remobilizing magnetite after ~498 Ma, likened to hypogene-supergene models (Fig. 14, p. 17), and restate it in the Conclusions.
steps.quote: a multistage upgrading processes involving the leaching of silica and subsequent magnetite remobilization

tree.answer: Yes: high-grade (TFe > 50 wt%) magnetite ore in an IF-hosted deposit
No: ore genesis is a past process known only from mineral, chemical and isotopic traces
Explain the ore genesis: stages, fluid source, timing
Yes: three literature models; magmatic versus non-magmatic fluid; I/S/A granite types; rift versus arc setting
Partly: S and O isotopes discriminate magmatic from meteoric/sulfate-derived fluid
Found, not set: outcrop and drill-core samples of a past event
Partly: concordant REE, O and S lines and analytical standards; no sensitivity tests or second deposit
Kept: meteoric-derived fluid leaching silica along dacite-related fractures after ~498 Ma

end.claim: The high-grade (T2) Zankan magnetite ores formed after ~498 Ma by leaching of silica from the original IF and remobilization and recrystallization of magnetite, by a fluid derived mainly from meteoric water that circulated along fractures created by the dacite-porphyry intrusion.

decisive_move.sentence: Excluding a directly magmatic ore fluid with the heavy pyrite δ34S values, backed by the magnetite δ18O, is what turns the shared REE pattern of ore and dacite into a meteoric-fluid leaching model.

gates.evidence: Action, partly: sampling and analyses were planned to separate ore-forming phases, following an inherited view that the high-grade ore is secondary (p. 3). The fluid-source rivals were posed only in the Discussion (p. 10). Claim, partly: the magmatic-fluid rival could have survived the S and O isotopes but did not (p. 10-11). The rest of the model (stages, setting, reactions) is assembled as a best explanation without a test it could fail. Registration, no: nothing is stated as fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: Inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS, LA-ICP-MS, MC-ICP-MS) for trace elements, U-Pb and Hf isotopes
Isotope ratio mass spectrometry (Finnigan MAT-253/251) for O and S isotopes
Balanced mineral-fluid reaction equations (R1-R3) to reason about fluid pH and redox

limits: The XML text supplies only captions, so body steps are located by printed page; quotes were checked against the PDF text. Internal inconsistency in the oxygen data: §4.4 (p. 8) gives T1 1.8-3.2‰ and T2 4.4-5.5‰, while Table 5 lists the high-grade (T2) samples at 1.8-3.2‰, and the Discussion (p. 10) gives T1 4.4-5.5‰ and T2 1.9-3.2‰. The coding follows the Discussion and table. The pyrite δ34S range is 19.1-27.3‰ in the Results and 19.1-28.2‰ in the Discussion, the latter including a sample from Chen (2012). The Conclusions cite 'Li et al., 2015' as a geochronology study, apparently a citation slip (inference). The age constraint rests on one U-Pb sample, with six zircons in the young group. The timing 'after 497.82 Ma' is inferred from veins in the dacite, not from dating the ore. The Li (2018) observations are coded as inherited on the inference that this is the first author's dissertation. Sub-claim statuses: U-Pb intrusion age, estimate_with_resolution; Hf crustal source, estimate_with_resolution; I-type classification, best_explanation; continental-arc setting, best_explanation; fluid reducing and acidic, best_explanation; microbial versus thermochemical sulfate reduction, left open. The comparison with Ding et al. (2021b) is coded as a replication performed here, because the paper does the comparison although the independent data are someone else's. There is no sensitivity analysis, no uncertainty propagation on isotopic interpretations, and no fluid-inclusion or temperature data. Data are available only on request. No review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded.

disagreements.target: Zhou et al. (2018) and Hu et al. (2020): the ZID reflects deposition in an early Cambrian seafloor hydrothermal system
disagreements.support: Field relations, the contrast between T1 and T2 REE and δ18O, and veins in the dacite are used to argue that the high-grade ore is a secondary, post-depositional product rather than a primary sedimentary-hydrothermal one.
disagreements.quote: it is apparent that the high-grade iron ore in the ZID is a product of the alteration of the primary IF

disagreements.target: Zhou et al. (2018): sulfur in Zankan pyrites sourced from a mixture of hydrothermal fluids and ambient seawater
disagreements.support: Heavy pyrite δ34S close to Cambrian seawater sulfate, together with O isotopes, is used to rule out a direct magmatic fluid for the high-grade ore.
disagreements.quote: Therefore, it is unlikely that the high-grade iron ore forming fluid was directly derived from the magma.

disagreements.target: Zheng et al. (2018): bimodal volcanics indicate an extensional event in the Taxkorgan region about 521 Ma
disagreements.support: The 497.82 Ma I-type dacite is taken as evidence for a continental-arc setting, which places rifting before subduction-related arc magmatism.
disagreements.quote: the extensional rift should be before a subduction-related arc system along the continental margin

disagreements.target: Previous studies defining IF-hosted high-grade ore as TFe > 60 wt% (hematite ores of Australia, South Africa, Brazil)
disagreements.support: Chinese magnetite IF ores are lower grade, so the paper adopts the Chinese national standard threshold.
disagreements.quote: in China high-grade magnetite ores are defined as having TFe >50 wt%

alternatives_considered.reason: Lacks peraluminous minerals; low ΣFeO/MgO; 10,000*Ga/Al (2.07-2.83) below the A-type minimum of 2.6

alternatives_considered.reason: Pyrite δ34S far heavier than mantle and close to seawater sulfate; light magnetite δ18O

alternatives_considered.chosen: Dacite-porphyry intrusion as the structural control on T2 ore
alternatives_considered.alternatives: The 505 ± 18 Ma granite near orebody IV
alternatives_considered.reason: The granite contains no magnetite-ferro actinolite veins and has no direct contact with the orebody

alternatives_considered.chosen: Sulfate reduction of basin-derived sulfate, with possible added magmatic H2S, as the pyrite sulfur source
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Microbial versus thermochemical sulfate reduction; dissolution of magmatic CO2 and H2S gases into meteoric water
alternatives_considered.reason: None given for choosing between microbial and thermochemical reduction; the final model invokes thermochemical reduction plus magmatic H2S

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Extensional rift (Zheng et al., 2018); early Paleozoic accretionary wedge (Zhou et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2018a, 2018b, 2019)
alternatives_considered.reason: The I-type character of the 497.82 Ma dacite

alternatives_considered.chosen: Multistage upgrading similar to hypogene-supergene models
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Syngenetic models; supergene and metamorphic models
alternatives_considered.reason: None given explicitly beyond similarity of the inferred processes
